mcqs.question: In Kafka's commit log model, what happens to a record after a consumer reads it?
options: It is immediately deleted from the log
It is marked as consumed and hidden from other consumer groups
It is moved to a separate "consumed" log
It stays in the log untouched — any number of consumers can read the same record independently
mcqs.explanation: Kafka never deletes or hides a record on read — it stays in the log until retention expires it, and any consumer can read it any number of times. There's no separate consumed log or per-group hiding mechanism.

mcqs.question: A Kafka topic has 12 partitions. What's the maximum number of consumers within a single consumer group that can actively read in parallel?
options: 12 — one consumer per partition; extras beyond that sit idle
Unlimited — Kafka lets any number of consumers read the same partition concurrently
1 — only one consumer per topic regardless of partition count
It depends only on the number of producers, not partitions
mcqs.explanation: Within one consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so parallelism caps out at the partition count — a 13th consumer would sit idle. Multiple consumers can't share a single partition within the same group, and producer count is unrelated.

mcqs.question: Two separate consumer groups, "fraud-detection" and "analytics," both read from the same Kafka topic. What happens?
options: Whichever group reads a record first prevents the other from reading it
Both groups read every record independently, each tracking its own offsets at its own pace
The topic must be duplicated into two separate topics, one per group
Only the group created first is allowed to consume
mcqs.explanation: Offsets are tracked per consumer group, so separate groups don't block or interfere with each other — each reads the full topic independently. No duplication or creation-order restriction is needed.

mcqs.question: Two events for the same user land on different Kafka partitions. What ordering guarantee applies between them?
options: Kafka guarantees they're processed in the order they were produced
Kafka guarantees they're processed in reverse order
None — Kafka only guarantees order within a single partition, not across partitions
Kafka guarantees order only if both events have the same timestamp
mcqs.explanation: Kafka's ordering guarantee is strictly per-partition; across partitions there's no defined relative order at all, regardless of timestamps. That's exactly why a consistent partition key matters for anything needing per-entity ordering.

mcqs.question: A topic is partitioned by "event_type," which has only 4 possible values, and one event type accounts for 90% of traffic. What happens?
options: Load balances evenly since Kafka rehashes keys internally
Nothing — partition count matters more than key cardinality
Consumers automatically split that one partition's load across each other
That one partition becomes a bottleneck no amount of extra partitions or consumers can relieve
mcqs.explanation: All records for the dominant event type hash to the same partition, so that partition absorbs 90% of the load regardless of how many partitions exist — and only one consumer can read a given partition at a time, so extra consumers can't help. Kafka doesn't rehash keys to rebalance skewed load.
